query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 10 atomic percent aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy promotes the formation of a stable Al2O3 surface layer at 1200 °C in air, reducing oxygen ingress and halving mass gain compared to an otherwise identical alloy without added Al.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with minimal Al content, fabricated via vacuum melting and homogenized to achieve a single-phase structure.
generation.intervention: Increase the Al content of the baseline RHEA to about 10 at.% during the initial alloy composition stage.
generation.conditions: Static air environment, 1200 °C, 50–100 hours of continuous exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, continuous Al2O3 oxide layer formed on the surface that impedes oxygen and metal ion diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature exposure, aluminum atoms selectively oxidize before other elements, creating an adherent alumina layer that acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced mass gain (approximately half) relative to the baseline alloy, indicating improved oxidation resistance under the specified high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Without sufficient Al, the RHEA grows less-protective oxides that allow faster oxygen penetration, resulting in higher mass gain and deeper internal oxidation.
generation.boundary: Above 1300 °C or in other oxidizing atmospheres (e.g., water vapor), oxide stability and adhesion may degrade, reducing the protective benefit of Al2O3.
generation.uncertainty: The precise protective effect and optimal Al content may vary with differing compositions and process routes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of RHEA samples via vacuum melting: one baseline alloy with minimal Al and one with ∼10 at.% Al. Oxidize each set at 1200 °C in air for 50–100 hours and compare mass-gain kinetics and oxide-layer morphology.
measurements: Mass gain measurements at fixed time intervals to track oxidation rate.
Cross-sectional microscopy (SEM/EDS) to evaluate oxide scale composition and thickness.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing RHEA does not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain or fails to form a continuous Al2O3 scale under these conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In recent years, high-temperature oxidation behavior has become the basic performance index and an important basis for judging the service performance and service life of an alloy, and the high-temperature oxidation performance of HEAs has also received much attention []. Y. Garip et al. [] studied the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the CoCrFeNiAlx series HEAs. The results indicated that the oxidation rates of all the oxidized HEAs increase with either increasing temperature or decreasing Al content, and the best oxidation resistance at temperatures of 800, 875, and 950 °C was observed with CoCrFeNiAl HEA. The oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi HEA at 1100 °C was investigated by Jie Lu et al. [] in 2021. They found that this HEA exhibits an extremely low oxidation rate and shows good resistance to oxide scale spallation. Butler and Liu [,] and others studied the oxidation behavior of AlxCrCoNiFe(Si) at high temperature. It was found that when the Al content (atomic fraction) is 10%, the oxidation kinetics of the alloy at 1050 °C conform to parabolic law [,], and the oxidation resistance at high temperature is the best among the various Al contents that were tested.

Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
